studies.title: Food knowledge depends upon the integrity of both sensory and functional properties: a VBM, TBSS and DTI tractography study.
studies.abstract: Food constitutes a fuel of life for human beings. It is therefore of chief importance that their recognition system readily identifies the most relevant properties of food by drawing on semantic memory. One of the most relevant properties to be considered is the level of processing impressed by humans on food. We hypothesized that recognition of raw food capitalizes on sensory properties and that of transformed food on functional properties, consistently with the hypothesis of a sensory-functional organization of semantic knowledge. To test this hypothesis, patients with Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, primary progressive aphasia, and healthy controls performed lexical-semantic tasks with food (raw and transformed) and non-food (living and nonliving) stimuli. Correlations between task performance and local grey matter concentration (VBM) and white matter fractional anisotropy (TBSS) led to two main findings. First, recognition of raw food and living things implicated occipital cortices, typically involved in processing sensory information and, second, recognition of processed food and nonliving things implicated the middle temporal gyrus and surrounding white matter tracts, regions that have been associated with functional properties. In conclusion, the present study confirms and extends the hypothesis of a sensory and a functional organization of semantic knowledge.

studies.title: Frontal and temporal lobe contributions to emotional enhancement of memory in behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease.
studies.abstract: Emotional events gain special priority in how they are remembered, with emotionally arousing events typically recalled more vividly and with greater confidence than non-emotional events. In dementia, memory and emotion processing are affected to varying degrees, however, whether emotional enhancement of memory for complex ecologically-valid events is differentially affected across dementia syndromes remains unclear, with previous studies examining effects of emotion on simple visual recognition only. Here, we examined memory for an emotionally arousing short story and a closely matched, emotionally neutral story in behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) (n = 13) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) (n = 14), and contrasted their performance with healthy controls (n = 12). Multiple-choice recognition memory for specific details of the story was assessed after a 1-h delay. While AD and control groups showed enhanced memory for the emotional story, the bvFTD group recalled a similar number of details from the emotional and neutral stories. Voxel-based morphometry analyses revealed emotional enhancement of memory correlated with distinct brain regions in each patient group. In AD, emotional enhancement was associated with integrity of the bilateral hippocampus, parahippocampal gyri, temporal fusiform gyrus and frontal pole, regions typically implicated in memory processes. In contrast in bvFTD, integrity of emotion processing regions, including the orbitofrontal cortex, right amygdala and right insula, correlated with the extent emotion enhanced memory. Our results reveal that integrity of frontal and temporal regions determine the quality and nature of emotional memories. While emotional enhancement of memory is present in mild AD, in bvFTD emotion does not facilitate memory retrieval for complex realistic events. This attenuation of emotional enhancement is due to degradation of emotion processing regions, which may be important for modulating levels of arousal in response to emotional events in these patients.

studies.title: Distinct patterns of cortical atrophy in ALS patients with or without dementia: an MRI VBM study.
studies.abstract: Voxel based morphometry (VBM) allows objective and automated detection of structural changes in brains of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). We investigated whether VBM could identify cortical atrophy from T1-weighted images obtained during routine 1.5T studies of ALS patients with various clinically defined phenotypes. For this purpose T1-weighted brain MRI was obtained at 1.5T during routine clinical study in neurologic disease controls (n = 15) and ALS patients (n = 88) categorized into four subgroups based on their clinical phenotypes: predominant upper motor neuron (UMN) dysfunction with or without corticospinal tract (CST) hyperintensity (ALS-CST+/-), combined UMN and prominent lower motor neuron (LMN) dysfunction (classic ALS), and frontotemporal dementia (ALS-FTD). VBM analysis of gray matter (GM) was carried out using FSL. Results demonstrated that clinically obtained brain MRI at 1.5T revealed significantly reduced GM volume in brains of only ALS-FTD patients and not of those with predominant UMN dysfunction or classic ALS, compared to neurologic disease controls. In conclusion, GM volume loss in motor and extramotor regions of only ALS patients with FTD and not of ALS patients without FTD suggests distinct sites of predominant pathology and possibly of disease onset. Brain volumetric measures supplemented by histopathological correlations and other neuroimaging techniques, such as diffusion tensor imaging, may provide insight into ALS pathophysiology.

studies.title: Frontotemporal dementia as a neural system disease.
studies.abstract: Some brain structures atrophic in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) belong to the rostral limbic system (RLS), that regulates context-dependent behaviors after evaluation of the motivational content of stimuli. The clinical manifestations of FTD are consistent with its impairment. Aim of this study was to assess whole brain morphology in FTD using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and voxel-based morphometry with statistic parametric mapping (SPM99) to test the hypothesis that the RLS might be specifically targeted by FTD. Nine FTD patients and 26 healthy controls underwent high resolution 3D MRI. SPM99 performed (a) spatial normalization to a customized template, (b) segmentation, (c) smoothing, (d) voxel-by-voxel comparison of gray matter between cases and controls. P was set at 0.05 corrected for multiple comparisons. All but one regions of the RLS (the periaqueductal gray) were atrophic in FTD. At P<0.001 uncorrected also the periaqueductal gray was atrophic. Atrophy outside the RLS was confined to a few voxels in the frontal and temporal gyri. FTD might be a neural-system disease where the RLS is predominantly damaged.

studies.title: Apolipoprotein E epsilon4 is associated with disease-specific effects on brain atrophy in Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia.
studies.abstract: Apolipoprotein epsilon4 (apoE4) has been strongly linked with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and contributes to several other neurological disorders. We investigated the influence of epsilon4 allele carrier status on the pattern of gray matter atrophy and disease severity in 51 patients with probable AD and 31 patients with behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), compared with 56 healthy controls. Voxel-based morphometry was performed by using statistical parametric mapping. The epsilon4 allele frequency was higher in the AD group (P < 0.001) than the controls but not in the bvFTD group. No differences in demographic or cognitive profiles were observed between epsilon4 allele carriers and noncarriers within any of the diagnostic groups. However, epsilon4 carrier status was associated with more severe brain atrophy in disease-specific regions compared with noncarriers in both AD and bvFTD. AD epsilon4 carriers showed greater atrophy in the bilateral parietal cortex and right hippocampus, and bvFTD epsilon4 carriers demonstrated greater atrophy in the bilateral medial, dorsolateral, and orbital frontal cortex, anterior insula, and cingulate cortex with right predominance. This regional epsilon4 effect is consistent with the hypothesis that apoE may affect the morphologic expression uniquely in different neurodegenerative diseases. The atrophy patterns in epsilon4 carriers may indicate that they are at greater risk for clinical progression.

studies.title: Converging evidence for the processing costs associated with ambiguous quantifier comprehension.
studies.abstract: Traditional neuroanatomic models of language comprehension have emphasized a core language network situated in peri-Sylvian cortex. More recent evidence appears to extend the neuroanatomic network beyond peri-Sylvian cortex to encompass other aspects of sentence processing. In this study, we evaluate the neuroanatomic basis for processing the ambiguity in doubly-quantified sentences. For example, a sentence like "All the dogs jumped in a lake" can be interpreted with a collective interpretation (e.g., several dogs jumping into a single lake) or a distributive interpretation (e.g., several dogs each jumping into a different lake). In Experiment 1, we used BOLD fMRI to investigate neuroanatomic recruitment by young adults during the interpretation of ambiguous doubly-quantified sentences in a sentence-picture verification task. We observed that young adults exhibited a processing cost associated with interpreting ambiguous sentences and this was related to frontal and parietal cortex recruitment. In Experiment 2, we investigate ambiguous sentence processing with the identical materials in non-aphasic patients with behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) who have frontal cortex disease and executive and decision-making limitations. bvFTD patients are insensitive to ambiguity associated with doubly-quantified sentences, and this is related to the magnitude of their frontal cortex disease. These studies provide converging evidence that cortical regions that extend beyond peri-Sylvian cortex help support the processing costs associated with the interpretation of ambiguous doubly-quantified sentences.

studies.title: What's in a name: voxel-based morphometric analyses of MRI and naming difficulty in Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia and corticobasal degeneration.
studies.abstract: Confrontation naming is impaired in neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and corticobasal degeneration (CBD). Some behavioural observations suggest a common source of impaired naming across these patient groups, while others find partially unique patterns of naming difficulty. We hypothesized that a large-scale neural network underlies naming, and that patterns of impaired naming in AD, FTD and CBD reflect cortical atrophy that interrupts this network in a manner that is partially shared and partially unique across these patient groups. We tested this hypothesis by correlating naming impairments with voxel-based morphometric (VBM) analyses of cortical atrophy in structural MRIs of 50 patients. We found significant naming deficits in all patient groups. Naming also correlated with lexical retrieval in all patient groups, including subgroups of patients with FTD. VBM analyses showed significant cortical atrophy, which was shared across AD, FTD and CBD patients in the left lateral temporal cortex; this area correlated with naming accuracy in all groups. Left lateral temporal atrophy thus appears to interfere with a lexical retrieval component of naming in AD, FTD and CBD. Impaired naming also correlated with semantic memory and visual perceptual-spatial functioning in specific groups of patients and, correspondingly, naming correlated with cortical atrophy in partially distinct neuroanatomical distributions in AD, FTD, CBD and subgroups of patients with FTD. These partially unique correlation profiles appear to reflect selective interruption of other components of the naming process, including semantic and visual perceptual-spatial functioning. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that a large-scale neural network supports naming, and that this network is interrupted in several distinct ways in patients with neurodegenerative diseases.

studies.title: Neural Substrates of Semantic Prospection - Evidence from the Dementias.
studies.abstract: The ability to envisage personally relevant events at a future time point represents an incredibly sophisticated cognitive endeavor and one that appears to be intimately linked to episodic memory integrity. Far less is known regarding the neurocognitive mechanisms underpinning the capacity to envisage non-personal future occurrences, known as semantic future thinking. Moreover the degree of overlap between the neural substrates supporting episodic and semantic forms of prospection remains unclear. To this end, we sought to investigate the capacity for episodic and semantic future thinking in Alzheimer's disease (n = 15) and disease-matched behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia (n = 15), neurodegenerative disorders characterized by significant medial temporal lobe (MTL) and frontal pathology. Participants completed an assessment of past and future thinking across personal (episodic) and non-personal (semantic) domains, as part of a larger neuropsychological battery investigating episodic and semantic processing, and their performance was contrasted with 20 age- and education-matched healthy older Controls. Participants underwent whole-brain T1-weighted structural imaging and voxel-based morphometry analysis was conducted to determine the relationship between gray matter integrity and episodic and semantic future thinking. Relative to Controls, both patient groups displayed marked future thinking impairments, extending across episodic and semantic domains. Analyses of covariance revealed that while episodic future thinking deficits could be explained solely in terms of episodic memory proficiency, semantic prospection deficits reflected the interplay between episodic and semantic processing. Distinct neural correlates emerged for each form of future simulation with differential involvement of prefrontal, lateral temporal, and medial temporal regions. Notably, the hippocampus was implicated irrespective of future thinking domain, with the suggestion of lateralization effects depending on the type of information being simulated. Whereas episodic future thinking related to right hippocampal integrity, semantic future thinking was found to relate to left hippocampal integrity. Our findings support previous observations of significant MTL involvement for semantic forms of prospection and point to distinct neurocognitive mechanisms which must be functional to support future-oriented forms of thought across personal and non-personal contexts.

studies.title: Neuroimaging patterns along the ALS-FTD spectrum: a multiparametric imaging study.
studies.abstract: Frontotemporal dementia is associated with considerable clinical, genetic and pathological heterogeneity. The objective of this study is to characterise the imaging signatures of the main FTD phenotypes along the ALS-FTD spectrum. A total of 100 participants underwent comprehensive multimodal neuroimaging, genetic testing and neuropsychological evaluation. Seven patients with behavioural variant FTD (bvFTD), 11 patients with non-fluent-variant primary progressive aphasia (nfvPPA), two patients with sematic-variant primary progressive aphasia(svPPA), 10 patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and FTD carrying the C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat (C9 + ALS-FTD), 10 patients with ALS-FTD without hexanucleotide repeats (C9-ALS-FTD), 20 ALS patients without behavioural or cognitive deficits (ALSnci) and 40 healthy controls (HC) were included in a prospective quantitative neuroimaging study. Phenotype-specific spatial patterns of pathology were identified along the ALS-FTD spectrum, highlighting a strikingly focal distribution of disease burden as opposed to global atrophy. Significant motor cortex and corticospinal tract degeneration was identified in both bvFTD and nfvPPA patients. C9-ALS-FTD patients exhibited widespread extramotor pathology and significant precentral gyrus atrophy compared to ALSnci patients. ROI analyses confirmed focal grey matter alterations in Broca's and Wernicke's area in language variant FTD cohorts. Our findings confirm that the clinical manifestations of FTD are underpinned by phenotype-specific patterns of white and grey matter degeneration.

studies.title: Executive and behavioral deficits share common neural substrates in frontotemporal lobar degeneration - a pilot FDG-PET study.
studies.abstract: Behavioral and executive dysfunctions are typical symptoms of frontotemporal lobar degeneration, associated with its subtypes frontotemporal and semantic dementia. Although both functions depend on the frontal lobes, no study has yet compared their neural correlates in frontotemporal lobar degeneration. Accordingly, we correlated clinical scores of behavioral and executive deficits with glucose utilization as measured by [(18)F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography in 17 patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration and 9 age- and sex-matched control subjects. Impairment in executive functions was measured by the Behavioral Assessment of the Dysexecutive Syndrome, a modified Stroop paradigm and/or the Tower of Toronto Test. Behavioral deficits were examined with the Neuropsychiatric Inventory. Executive dysfunction was correlated with diminished glucose utilization in frontomedial and frontolateral cortices. Brain regions included the anterior cingulate and midcingulate gyri, anterior medial frontal cortex, and left frontolateral cortex. Behavioral deficits were associated with mainly frontomedial networks, particularly the anterior medial frontal cortex, gyrus rectus, and area subcallosa. Our pilot study reveals partially overlapping neural correlates of executive and behavioral dysfunction in frontotemporal lobar degeneration. The results suggest that some behavioral deficits, namely disinhibition and appetite and eating abnormalities, are particularly related to executive dysfunction. This hypothesis might be further explored in studies involving larger patient groups.

studies.title: A standardized [18F]-FDG-PET template for spatial normalization in statistical parametric mapping of dementia.
studies.abstract: [18F]-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a widely used diagnostic tool that can detect and quantify pathophysiology, as assessed through changes in cerebral glucose metabolism. [18F]-FDG PET scans can be analyzed using voxel-based statistical methods such as Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM) that provide statistical maps of brain abnormalities in single patients. In order to perform SPM, a "spatial normalization" of an individual's PET scan is required to match a reference PET template. The PET template currently used for SPM normalization is based on [15O]-H2O images and does not resemble either the specific metabolic features of [18F]-FDG brain scans or the specific morphological characteristics of individual brains affected by neurodegeneration. Thus, our aim was to create a new [18F]-FDG PET aging and dementia-specific template for spatial normalization, based on images derived from both age-matched controls and patients. We hypothesized that this template would increase spatial normalization accuracy and thereby preserve crucial information for research and diagnostic purposes. We investigated the statistical sensitivity and registration accuracy of normalization procedures based on the standard and new template-at the single-subject and group level-independently for subjects with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), probable Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). We found a significant statistical effect of the population-specific FDG template-based normalisation in key anatomical regions for each dementia subtype, suggesting that spatial normalization with the new template provides more accurate estimates of metabolic abnormalities for single-subject and group analysis, and therefore, a more effective diagnostic measure.

studies.title: False Recognition in Behavioral Variant Frontotemporal Dementia and Alzheimer's Disease-Disinhibition or Amnesia?
studies.abstract: Episodic memory recall processes in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) can be similarly impaired, whereas recognition performance is more variable. A potential reason for this variability could be false-positive errors made on recognition trials and whether these errors are due to amnesia per se or a general over-endorsement of recognition items regardless of memory. The current study addressed this issue by analysing recognition performance on the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (RAVLT) in 39 bvFTD, 77 AD and 61 control participants from two centers (India, Australia), as well as disinhibition assessed using the Hayling test. Whereas both AD and bvFTD patients were comparably impaired on delayed recall, bvFTD patients showed intact recognition performance in terms of the number of correct hits. However, both patient groups endorsed significantly more false-positives than controls, and bvFTD and AD patients scored equally poorly on a sensitivity index (correct hits-false-positives). Furthermore, measures of disinhibition were significantly associated with false positives in both groups, with a stronger relationship with false-positives in bvFTD. Voxel-based morphometry analyses revealed similar neural correlates of false positive endorsement across bvFTD and AD, with both patient groups showing involvement of prefrontal and Papez circuitry regions, such as medial temporal and thalamic regions, and a DTI analysis detected an emerging but non-significant trend between false positives and decreased fornix integrity in bvFTD only. These findings suggest that false-positive errors on recognition tests relate to similar mechanisms in bvFTD and AD, reflecting deficits in episodic memory processes and disinhibition. These findings highlight that current memory tests are not sufficient to accurately distinguish between bvFTD and AD patients.

studies.title: The Effect of Gray Matter ICA and Coefficient of Variation Mapping of BOLD Data on the Detection of Functional Connectivity Changes in Alzheimer's Disease and bvFTD.
studies.abstract: Resting-state fMRI results in neurodegenerative diseases have been somewhat conflicting. This may be due to complex partial volume effects of CSF in BOLD signal in patients with brain atrophy. To encounter this problem, we used a coefficient of variation (CV) map to highlight artifacts in the data, followed by analysis of gray matter voxels in order to minimize brain volume effects between groups. The effects of these measures were compared to whole brain ICA dual regression results in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD). 23 AD patients, 21 bvFTD patients and 25 healthy controls were included. The quality of the data was controlled by CV mapping. For detecting functional connectivity (FC) differences whole brain ICA (wbICA) and also segmented gray matter ICA (gmICA) followed by dual regression were conducted, both of which were performed both before and after data quality control. Decreased FC was detected in posterior DMN in the AD group and in the Salience network in the bvFTD group after combining CV quality control with gmICA. Before CV quality control, the decreased connectivity finding was not detectable in gmICA in neither of the groups. Same finding recurred when exclusion was based on randomization. The subjects excluded due to artifacts noticed in the CV maps had significantly lower temporal signal-to-noise ratio than the included subjects. Data quality measure CV is an effective tool in detecting artifacts from resting state analysis. CV reflects temporal dispersion of the BOLD signal stability and may thus be most helpful for spatial ICA, which has a blind spot in spatially correlating widespread artifacts. CV mapping in conjunction with gmICA yields results suiting previous findings both in AD and bvFTD.

studies.title: Getting on the same page: the neural basis for social coordination deficits in behavioral variant frontotemporal degeneration.
studies.abstract: For social interactions to be successful, individuals must establish shared mental representations that allow them to reach a common understanding and "get on the same page". We refer to this process as social coordination. While examples of social coordination are ubiquitous in daily life, relatively little is known about the neuroanatomic basis of this complex behavior. This is particularly true in a language context, as previous studies have used overly complex paradigms to study this. Although traditional views of language processing and the recent interactive-alignment account of conversation focus on peri-Sylvian regions, our model of social coordination predicts prefrontal involvement. To test this hypothesis, we examine the neural basis of social coordination during conversational exchanges in non-aphasic patients with behavioral variant frontotemporal degeneration (bvFTD). bvFTD patients show impairments in executive function and social comportment due to disease in frontal and anterior temporal regions. To investigate social coordination in bvFTD, we developed a novel language-based task that assesses patients' ability to convey an object's description to a conversational partner. Experimental conditions manipulated the amount of information shared by the participant and the conversational partner, and the associated working memory demands. Our results indicate that, although patients did not have difficulty identifying the features of the objects, they did produce descriptions that included insufficient or inappropriate adjectives and thus struggled to communicate effectively. Impaired performance was related to gray matter atrophy particularly in medial prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortices. Our findings suggest an important role for non-language brain areas that belong to a large-scale neurocognitive network for social coordination.

studies.title: The orbitofrontal cortex is involved in emotional enhancement of memory: evidence from the dementias.
studies.abstract: The enhancing effect of emotion on subsequent memory retrieval is well established. Patients with frontotemporal dementia show profound emotion processing difficulties, yet the extent to which such deficits attenuate emotional enhancement of memory remains unknown. Here, we studied the intersection between emotion and memory using a visual forced-choice recognition test for negative and neutral stimuli in 34 patients with frontotemporal dementia compared with 10 patients with Alzheimer's disease and 15 control subjects. Control subjects and patients with Alzheimer's disease recognized more emotional than neutral items, as demonstrated by a significant interaction between emotion and memory for true recognition. This emotional enhancement effect was notably absent in the frontotemporal dementia cohort, with comparable recognition performance regardless of emotional content. Voxel-based morphometry analyses revealed distinct neural substrates for overall memory versus emotional memory performance. Overall memory performance correlated with the hippocampus, precuneus and posterior cingulate, regions crucial for successful episodic memory performance. Emotional enhancement of memory, by contrast, was associated exclusively with the integrity of the right orbitofrontal and subcallosal cortex. Our findings demonstrate differential disruption of emotional enhancement of memory in neurodegenerative disorders, and point toward the potentially pivotal role of the orbitofrontal cortex in supporting the successful retrieval of emotionally charged negative stimuli.

studies.title: Are frontal cognitive and atrophy patterns different in PSP and bvFTD? A comparative neuropsychological and VBM study.
studies.abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTD) are two clinicohistological entities that share a severe prefrontal syndrome. To what extent do the cognitive syndrome and the location of the underlying brain atrophy unify or segregate these entities? Here, we examined the clinical and radiological patterns of frontal involvement and the neural bases of the cognitive dysfunctions observed in the Richardson form of PSP and the behavioral variant of FTD (bvFTD). The cognitive profile and grey and white matter volume of PSP (n = 19) and bvFTD (n = 16) patients and control participants (n = 18) were compared using a standard battery of neuropsychological tests and voxel-based morphometry (VBM), respectively. Analyses of correlations between neuropsychological and morphometric data were additionally performed. The severity and qualitative pattern of cognitive dysfunction was globally similar between the two patient groups. Grey matter volume was decreased in widespread frontal areas and in the temporal uncus in bvFTD, while it was decreased in the frontal and temporal lobes as well as in the thalamus in PSP. We also found an unexpected involvement of the frontal rectal gyrus in PSP patients compared to controls. Correlation analyses yielded different results in the two groups, with no area showing significant correlations in PSP patients, while several frontal and some temporal areas did so in bvFTD patients. In spite of minor neuropsychological and morphological differences, this study shows that the patterns of cognitive dysfunction and atrophy are very similar in PSP and bvFTD. However, executive dysfunction in these diseases may stem from partially divergent cortical and subcortical neural circuits.

studies.title: Fear conditioning in frontotemporal lobar degeneration and Alzheimer's disease.
studies.abstract: Emotional blunting and abnormal processing of rewards and punishments represent early features of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD). Better understanding of the physiological underpinnings of these emotional changes can be facilitated by the use of classical psychology approaches. Fear conditioning (FC) is an extensively used paradigm for studying emotional processing that has rarely been applied to the study of dementia. We studied FC in controls (n = 25), Alzheimer's disease (n = 25) and FTLD (n = 25). A neutral stimulus (coloured square on a computer screen) was repeatedly paired with a 1 s burst of 100 db white noise. Change in skin conductance response to the neutral stimulus was used to measure conditioning. Physiological-anatomical correlations were examined using voxel-based morphometry (VBM). Both patient groups showed impaired acquisition of conditioned responses. However, the basis for this deficit appeared to differ between groups. In Alzheimer's disease, impaired FC occurred despite normal electrodermal responses to the aversive stimulus. In contrast, FTLD patients showed reduced skin conductance responses to the aversive stimulus, which contributed significantly to their FC deficit. VBM identified correlations with physiological reactivity in the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, orbitofrontal cortex and insula. These data indicate that Alzheimer's disease and FTLD both show abnormalities in emotional learning, but they suggest that in FTLD this is associated with a deficit in basic electrodermal response to aversive stimuli, consistent with the emotional blunting described with this disorder. Deficits in responses to aversive stimuli could contribute to both the behavioural and cognitive features of FTLD and Alzheimer's disease. Further study of FC in humans and animal models of dementia could provide a valuable window into these symptoms.

studies.title: Predominant ventromedial frontopolar metabolic impairment in frontotemporal dementia.
studies.abstract: In a multicenter study, FDG-PET images in a population of 29 patients with frontotemporal dementia (FTD) were compared to controls with similar age from each center. A conjunction analysis led to identification of the ventromedial frontopolar cortex as the single region affected in each and every FTD patients. This precise regional metabolic impairment should be integrated with recent neuropsychological researches, such as those showing that the ventromedial frontal cortex is critically involved in decision-making processes based on personal experience, feelings of rightness or social knowledge, processes that are characteristically impaired in FTD.

studies.title: Anatomic correlates of stereotypies in frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
studies.abstract: Stereotypies are common in frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) however the anatomical correlates of stereotypies are unknown. We therefore set out to compare patterns of grey matter volume loss in FTLD subjects with and without stereotypies. Subjects with a diagnosis of FTLD that met international consensus criteria were prospectively recruited and separated into those with and without stereotypies. MRI and cognitive measures were obtained and voxel-based morphometry was used to assess the patterns of grey matter volume loss in those with and without stereotypies, compared to a group of age- and gender-matched controls. Demographic and clinical features were similar between subjects with and without stereotypies. FTLD subjects with stereotypies had greater volume loss in the striatum compared to those without stereotypies. Those without stereotypies showed a more widespread and typical pattern of cortical frontotemporal loss. Stereotypies in FTLD are therefore associated with a greater proportion of striatal to cortical volume loss than those without stereotypies.

studies.title: Non-Fluent Speech in Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration.
studies.abstract: We investigated the cognitive and neural bases of impaired speech fluency, a central feature of primary progressive aphasia. Speech fluency was assessed in 35 patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) who presented with progressive non-fluent aphasia (PNFA, n=11), semantic dementia (SemD, n=12), or a social and executive disorder without aphasia (SOC/EXEC, n=12). Fluency was quantified as the number of words per minute in an extended, semi-structured speech sample. This was related to language characteristics of the speech sample and to neuropsychological measures. PNFA patients were significantly less fluent than controls and other FTLD patients. Fluency correlated with grammatical expression but not with speech errors or executive difficulty. SemD and SOC/EXEC patients were also less fluent than controls. In SemD, fluency was associated with semantically limited content. In SOC/EXEC, fluency was associated with executive limitations. Voxel-based morphometry analyses of high-resolution MRI related fluency to gray matter volume in left inferior frontal, insula, and superior temporal regions for the entire cohort of FTLD patients. This region overlapped partially distinct atrophic areas in each FTLD subgroup. It thus appears to play a crucial role in speech fluency, which can be interrupted in different ways in different FTLD subgroups.

studies.fulltext_screening_reason: This study reports voxel-based morphometry (VBM) analyses relating gray matter atrophy to speech fluency in FTLD subgroups. The cohort includes a social/executive (SOC/EXEC) subgroup characterized by social comportment and executive deficits consistent with behavioral-variant FTD. Imaging was performed on a subset (n=22 patients; SOC/EXEC n=9) and contrasted against age-matched controls (n=31) using whole-brain, voxelwise SPM analyses in MNI space; subgroup-specific atrophy maps and overlaps with fluency-related voxels are reported in figures and tables. Sample sizes meet the >=6 patient and >=6 control thresholds for the SOC/EXEC imaging subgroup. Thus the study provides whole-brain, between-group VBM results for a bvFTD-like group. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only analysis, review article, disallowed modality) are met. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion, appendices).

No exclusion criteria apply (not a review; not ROI-only; no disallowed exclusive modality). Full text appears complete (intro, methods, results, discussion). Thus the paper meets all inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria were violated.

This study meets all required inclusion criteria: (I3) it uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM) for structural MRI analyses; (I4) includes a clinically diagnosed bvFTD group (16 probable bvFTD patients diagnosed by expert consensus); (I5) sample sizes meet thresholds (16 bvFTD patients and 22 healthy controls); (I6) reports between-group VBM contrasts comparing bvFTD to controls (whole-brain two-sample comparisons with explicit statistical thresholds and MNI normalization described); (I7) presents whole-brain, group-level voxelwise results for the target bvFTD group (FWE-corrected results reported, and comparisons bvFTD>controls and bvFTD>BD described); (I8) results/coordinates are indicated as reported in figures/tables (methods state normalization to MNI space and VBM outputs). The provided full text includes introduction, methods, results and discussion; core article content is present (fulltext_incomplete=false). No exclusion criteria apply. Overall, the paper provides whole-brain VBM evidence for bvFTD vs controls and is eligible for inclusion in the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical FDG-PET study of clinically diagnosed probable bvFTD patients (n=17) that reports voxel-wise, whole-brain SPM analyses (single-subject comparisons to a normative database and group-level one-sample t-tests) with results presented in SPM/MNI space. Imaging modality = FDG-PET; sample meets size requirement; group-level whole-brain voxelwise results from the bvFTD sample are described and overlaid on an MNI template. No exclusion criteria (e.g., review, ROI-only, non-empirical methods, disallowed modalities, or comorbid psychiatric/neurologic confounds) are met. Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore the study meets the review inclusion criteria.

This is an empirical VBM study that includes a clearly defined bvFTD patient group (n=22) and age-matched controls (n=38). The paper uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM) (I3) and reports voxelwise, whole-brain (voxelwise GLM with permutation testing) group contrasts between bvFTD and controls with MNI coordinates and cluster thresholds provided (I6, I7). Sample sizes meet the minimum (I5). The bvFTD group is reported separately (not pooled) and the paper provides group-level whole-brain results in the main text and supplementary tables/figures (I4, I8). Full text provided includes introduction, methods, results, discussion, and tables/figures descriptions, so fulltext appears complete. No exclusion criteria apply. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis and should be INCLUDED.

Exclusion applied: E9 (study reports only cortical thickness methods). Inclusion met: I4 (clinically diagnosed bvFTD sample included), I5 (sufficient sample sizes: 37 bvFTD, 33 controls), I7 (whole-brain vertex-wise cortical thickness analyses performed), I8 (results reported with supplementary material). Inclusion not met: I3 (required imaging modality VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET — this study used structural MRI cortical thickness and subcortical volumetry via FreeSurfer), I6 (unclear/no between-group results reported in a defined stereotactic coordinate space such as MNI/Talairach; vertex-wise surface results do not provide standard voxel coordinates in the paper text). The full text appears complete. Therefore the study must be excluded because it uses cortical thickness methods (excluded by E9) and does not meet the required imaging modalities (I3).

This study includes FDG-PET (I3), includes clinically diagnosed behavioural variant FTD patients (I4) with adequate sample sizes (20 FTD patients; controls n=38) satisfying I5. However, the paper reports visual assessment of individual Z-maps and reader-based diagnostic performance rather than reporting any group-level, whole-brain voxelwise between-group contrasts in MNI/Talairach space (no coordinates or voxelwise statistical maps for bvFTD vs controls are provided). Therefore it does not meet I6 and I7 (no group-level voxelwise contrast or whole-brain results for the target sample). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present). No exclusion criteria were triggered.

This study includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients and uses resting-state fMRI and DTI (I3,I4) with adequate sample sizes (bvFTD n=12; controls n=18) (I5). However, it does not report any whole-brain, voxelwise group-level results in a standard stereotactic space (MNI/Talairach): diffusion results are tract-specific (DTI/tractography) and functional results are ROI-to-ROI DMN connectivity (ROI-based) with non-significant between-group voxelwise findings. Therefore it fails to meet I6 and I7 (no between-group voxelwise coordinates/whole-brain maps for bvFTD vs controls). Because the paper reports only tract-based DTI and ROI/seed-based functional connectivity (no voxelwise VBM/fMRI/FDG-PET coordinate results), it meets exclusion criteria E6 (only ROI analyses / no whole-brain results) and E9 (reports DTI and seed/ROI FC rather than whole-brain voxelwise modalities required). Full text appears complete. Exclusion based on E6 and E9.

This study used DTI tractography and a targeted VBM approach applied to an anterior cingulate mask rather than reporting whole-brain, voxelwise group comparisons in stereotactic space with coordinates. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (uses VBM method—FSL-VBM modification applied), I4 (clinically diagnosed bvFTD sample), I5 (≥6 patients and ≥6 controls). Inclusion criteria NOT met: I6 (no reported between-group contrast results in defined stereotactic space with coordinates/MNI or Talairach reported), I7 (no group-level whole-brain voxelwise results—analyses were ROI/masked to the ACC and tract-specific). Exclusion criteria applied: E6 (study reports only ROI/tract-based analyses with no whole-brain voxelwise results). Full text appears complete (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion). Therefore excluded for failing whole-brain/voxelwise reporting requirements.

Excluded because the paper does not report a between-group voxelwise contrast comparing the bvFTD group to healthy controls in a defined stereotactic space (MNI/Talairach). The study uses FDG-PET (I3), includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients (n=37) (I4, I5), and reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise regression results within the bvFTD sample (I7) described in the text/figures (I8). However, it does not present at least one between-group contrast of bvFTD versus controls (I6 not met). No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) are triggered. Full text appears complete (fulltext_incomplete=false).

This study is excluded because the VBM analyses were constrained to a fronto-striatal ROI mask (region-of-interest voxelwise analysis) rather than reporting whole-brain, group-level voxelwise results. Thus it meets exclusion criterion E6 (ROI-only analyses with no whole-brain results). Inclusion criteria met: I3 (VBM used), I4 (bvFTD sample clinically diagnosed, n=11), I5 (bvFTD n>=6 and controls n>=6), I6 (between-group contrasts reported in stereotactic space comparing bvFTD to controls). Inclusion criteria not met: I7 (does not report at least one whole-brain, voxelwise group-level result for the target sample; analyses were ROI-restricted). Full text appears complete. Therefore the paper must be excluded from the meta-analysis because it provides only ROI-limited voxelwise findings rather than qualifying whole-brain results required by the review.

Full text is complete. Exclusion rationale: No relevant imaging modality (I3 not met) — the study uses longitudinal structural MRI with tensor-based morphometry/boundary-shift integral, not VBM, task/resting fMRI, or FDG-PET. No bvFTD vs healthy-control voxelwise contrasts in stereotactic space (I6 and I7 not met) — the paper reports voxelwise comparisons across genetic FTD groups and regional atrophy rates, and a secondary analysis limited to bvFTD, but it does not present a between-group (bvFTD vs controls) whole-brain voxelwise contrast in MNI/Talairach coordinates. Inclusion criteria met: I4 (includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD subjects) and I5 (patient group sizes ≥6). Inclusion criteria not met: I3, I6, I7. No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) directly apply. Therefore study must be excluded.

This is an empirical VBM study that includes a clinically diagnosed bvFTD group (n=24) and healthy controls (n=179), both exceeding the minimum sample size. The paper reports whole-brain, voxelwise VBM results including between-group contrasts (bvFTD vs controls) with MNI coordinates, and additionally reports whole-brain interaction and region coordinates. Methods, results, and discussion are present and complete. No exclusion criteria apply (not a review, not ROI-only, not non-empirical, not an unsupported imaging modality). Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical study that used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) whole-brain analyses to examine neural correlates of empathy in clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients. The sample includes 24 bvFTD patients and 22 healthy controls (both >6). The paper reports voxel-wise, whole-brain between-group contrasts and covariate analyses with anatomical results reported in MNI stereotaxic space (coordinates and tables/figures referenced). The full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. No exclusion criteria (e.g., review article, ROI-only analysis, excluded comorbid samples, non-empirical methods) are met. Therefore the study meets all required inclusion criteria (I3, I4, I5, I6, I7, I8) and is suitable for inclusion in the meta-analysis focused on bvFTD VBM studies.

This study reports empirical imaging and behavioral data on clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients (n=14) and age-matched controls (n=19). It includes voxel-based morphometry (VBM) analyses and resting-state fMRI connectivity, reports whole-brain, voxelwise group contrasts and coordinates (e.g., ATL [-45,13,-37]; IFG [-52,2,14]) in standard space, and provides group-level results comparing bvFTD to controls. Sample sizes meet thresholds. Full article text (intro, methods, results, discussion) is present. No exclusion criteria (reviews, ROI-only, comorbid psychiatric/other dementia confounds, non-empirical, or limited-to-seed-only methods) apply based on provided content.

This is an empirical, whole-brain VBM study of behavioral variant FTD (bvFTD). It uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM) (I3), includes a clinically diagnosed bvFTD sample (n=14) (I4) with healthy controls (n=18) and an AD group (n=15) meeting the sample size threshold (I5). The paper reports between-group voxelwise contrasts and covariate analyses in MNI space (methods state MNI registration) comparing bvFTD to controls/AD (I6), and provides whole-brain, group-level voxelwise results (VBM and TBSS) clearly attributed to the bvFTD group (I7). Results are presented in tables/figures (including supplementary tables/figures and cluster coordinates) (I8). No exclusion criteria apply (not a review, not ROI-only, not non-empirical, no pooling of bvFTD with other disorders for the reported contrasts). Full text appears complete. Based on these points, the study meets all inclusion criteria and is eligible for inclusion in the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical study with FDG-PET and MRI in a clinically characterized bvFTD cohort, but it does not report any voxelwise/whole-brain (MNI/Talairach) between-group coordinate results. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (FDG-PET used), I4 (includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients), I5 (patient group N=27 ≥6). Inclusion criteria not met: I6 (no between-group contrast in MNI/Talairach space comparing bvFTD to controls), I7 (no group-level whole-brain/voxelwise results), I8 (no whole-brain results reported as coordinates/figures in standard space). No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) were directly triggered. Therefore exclude because key whole-brain/voxelwise reporting requirements (I6–I8) are not satisfied.

Exclusion (E6) applies: the study performs ROI-based network analyses using AAL parcellation and MST on regionwise wavelet correlation matrices; it does not report voxelwise, whole-brain group-level results in a stereotactic coordinate space (MNI/Talairach). Inclusion criteria met: I3 (resting-state fMRI used), I4 (clinically diagnosed bvFTD sample), I5 (n=41 bvFTD, n=39 controls). Inclusion criteria not met: I6 and I7 (no between-group voxelwise contrasts reported in MNI/Talairach coordinates; results are region/ROI-level and graph-based rather than whole-brain voxelwise statistical maps). Full text appears complete; decision based on methods and results sections describing ROI-based analyses without coordinate tables or voxelwise group contrasts.

The study should be excluded because it reports Freesurfer ROI-based structural volume analyses rather than VBM, task/resting fMRI, or FDG-PET, and it does not present whole-brain voxelwise (MNI/Talairach) group-level results. Exclusion criterion met: E6 (ROI-only analyses with no whole-brain results). Inclusion criteria met: I4 (includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients) and I5 (bvFTD group n=48 and controls n=94, both ≥6). Inclusion criteria not met: I3 (imaging modality is not VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET), I6 (no between-group contrasts reported in defined stereotactic space), and I7 (no whole-brain voxelwise group-level results). Full text appears complete with methods, results, and discussion, so fulltext_incomplete=false. Given these mismatches with required imaging and whole-brain reporting, the study does not qualify for inclusion in this meta-analysis.

Exclusion IDs met: E6 (study reports ROI/parcellation analyses without whole-brain voxelwise results) and E9 (reports surface-based cortical volumes/parcellation rather than qualifying modalities). Inclusion IDs met: I4 (includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients; n=32) and I5 (patient and control groups both ≥6 participants). Inclusion IDs NOT met: I3 (does not use VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET; uses Freesurfer regional volumes), I6 (no between-group voxelwise contrast reported in MNI/Talairach space comparing bvFTD vs controls), and I7 (no whole-brain voxelwise group-level results). The full text is complete for screening. Because the imaging modality and whole-brain voxelwise reporting requirements are not satisfied, the study does not meet the meta-analysis inclusion criteria.

This study reports voxel-wise, whole-brain SPM analyses using FDG-PET and optimized VBM-MRI in a clinically diagnosed FTD sample (13 patients) with semantic dementia and progressive nonfluent aphasia specifically excluded (consistent with behavioral-variant FTD recruitment). Imaging modalities match (FDG-PET and VBM). Sample sizes meet the minimum (13 FTD, 20 controls). Data were normalized to MNI space and voxel-by-voxel group contrasts are reported (tables/figures) comparing FTD to controls and to AD — satisfying whole-brain, group-level voxelwise results in a defined stereotactic space. Full text includes methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria from the review appear to be violated. Therefore the paper meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8.

The study is excluded because it does not use the required imaging modalities (VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET) required by I3, and it does not report between-group coordinates in a defined stereotactic space (MNI/Talairach) required by I6. It does include clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients (n=9) and controls (n=18) satisfying I4 and I5, and it reports whole-brain voxelwise DTI (TBSS) results (I7). However, the meta-analysis requires specific modalities (I3), which are absent (study uses DTI, ASL perfusion, and structural ROI volumetry), and no between-group coordinate-based contrasts for bvFTD vs controls are provided (I6 not met). Full text appears complete.

Although the study uses FDG-PET (I3), includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients (I4), and has >=6 patients and >=6 controls (I5), it does not provide a group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) contrast that is specific to a bvFTD-only group versus controls. The reported voxelwise maps and group analyses are performed on a mixed FTD patient sample (multiple FTD subtypes pooled), and group-level comparisons are presented mainly as ROI analyses. Therefore inclusion criteria I6 and I7 (bvFTD-only between-group voxelwise contrast and whole-brain group-level voxelwise result from the target sample) are not met. Full text appears complete. No exclusion criteria from the list are triggered.

This VBM study includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients (I4) using VBM imaging (I3) with >=6 patients (n=20) (I5). However, it does not report any between-group voxelwise contrasts comparing bvFTD to controls (no bvFTD vs control results), so inclusion criteria I6 is not met. Analyses are voxelwise but were restricted to a frontal mask rather than reporting whole-brain, group-level voxelwise results, so I7 (whole-brain evidence) is not met. Therefore it fails required inclusion criteria. Exclusion criterion E6 applies because the paper provides masked/region-restricted voxelwise analyses without whole-brain results. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present).

This is a methods/design paper describing an ongoing cohort (LOF study) and does not report empirical whole-brain voxelwise comparisons or coordinate results for clinically diagnosed bvFTD versus controls. Exclusion criteria met: E8 (non-empirical/methods-only paper without original voxelwise imaging results). Inclusion criteria met: I3 (FDG-PET is included as an imaging modality in the study design) and I5 (sample size exceeds 6 participants — cohort includes ~130 patients). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (participants are a symptom-based LOF cohort, not a sample of clinically diagnosed bvFTD/Pick’s disease patients), I6 (no reported between-group contrasts in MNI/Talairach space comparing bvFTD to controls), and I7 (no group-level whole-brain voxelwise results are reported). Full text appears complete (contains background, methods, and discussion), but lacks the required empirical imaging results for inclusion in the meta-analysis.

Although the study uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients (total n=252 across controls and three dementia syndromes), it does not report any whole-brain, voxelwise between-group contrast that compares bvFTD patients alone to healthy controls. The reported whole-brain VBM results (with MNI coordinates) are for a Val allele dose linear contrast across all subjects (controls + AD + bvFTD + SemD) rather than a bvFTD vs control contrast where bvFTD is not pooled with other patient groups. Therefore the study fails to meet I6 (bvFTD-specific between-group contrast with coordinates) and I7 (group-level, whole-brain voxelwise result clearly identified as coming from the bvFTD sample). I3 (VBM modality), I4 (includes bvFTD sample), and I5 (adequate sample size overall and implied per-group sizes) are satisfied. Full text appears complete. No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) were met.

This study is excluded because it reports cortical thickness (surface-based volumetric) analyses rather than one of the eligible imaging modalities. Exclusion criteria met: E9 (study reports cortical thickness methods). Inclusion criteria satisfied: I4 (clinically diagnosed bvFTD sample), I5 (bvFTD n=17 and controls n=22, both >=6), I6 (reports between-group contrast comparing bvFTD to controls using voxelwise analyses and peak voxels), I7 (reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise cortical-thickness results). Inclusion criteria not met: I3 (imaging modality is not VBM, fMRI, or FDG-PET). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present). Because E9 is met (cortical thickness only), the study must be excluded per review rules.

Met inclusion criteria: I3 (used VBM), I4 (included clinically diagnosed bv-FTD patients, n=27), I5 (patient groups and controls each >=6; controls n=14). Not met: I6 and I7 — the provided full text does not report any between-group, voxelwise contrast (bvFTD versus controls) with coordinates in a defined stereotactic space clearly identified as coming from the bvFTD group alone. The main whole-brain VBM finding reported is a correlational analysis across all patient groups (not a bvFTD-specific between-group contrast), and the authors note that correlational analyses within each diagnostic group did not yield results surviving correction. Although the methods state that patient-group vs control comparisons were performed and some results are referenced as being in online supplementary materials, those bvFTD-versus-control voxelwise coordinates/results are not presented in the provided full text. No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) are triggered based on the available content.

The full text reports empirical neuroimaging data in a clinically diagnosed bvFTD cohort using voxel-based morphometry and task-based fMRI (satisfies I3). The sample includes >6 bvFTD patients (10 behavioral analyses, 8 in neuroimaging) and 16 controls (satisfies I4 and I5). The paper reports between-group, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (VBM and fMRI) comparing bvFTD patients to controls, with results presented in tables/figures and coordinates (satisfies I6, I7, I8). No exclusion criteria apply: this is not a review/meta-analysis, includes whole-brain analyses (not ROI-only), and does not report only seed-based FC/DTI/cortical thickness; there is no indication of comorbid psychiatric diagnoses or other dementia pooling that would violate E7. The provided full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so fulltext_incomplete=false.

This study meets I3 (uses VBM, resting-state fMRI, and 18F-FDG PET), I4 (includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients; n=11), and I5 (bvFTD group size ≥6). However, it does not meet I6 or I7: there is no healthy/control group reported for between-group contrasts versus bvFTD, and the paper does not present group-level whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (in MNI/Talairach space) comparing bvFTD to controls. Analyses are restricted to predefined ROI cores (voxelwise measures within those ROIs) and multivariate SVM classification; results are reported as classification accuracies rather than whole-brain coordinate-based between-group contrasts. Therefore the study reports only ROI-limited results with no qualifying whole-brain group contrasts and falls under exclusion E6 (only ROI analyses with no whole-brain results). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This study used VBM (I3), included a clinically diagnosed bvFTD group (n=13, I4), and had adequate sample sizes for patients and controls (bvFTD n=13; controls n=20, I5). However, the VBM analyses reported are correlational within a combined patient cohort and significant effects were reported only within pre-specified regions of interest; no between-group voxelwise contrasts comparing bvFTD versus controls in standard stereotactic space (MNI/Talairach) are presented, and no whole-brain group-level voxelwise results for the bvFTD group are reported. Therefore inclusion criteria I6 and I7 are not met. This meets exclusion criterion E6 (reports only ROI findings / no qualifying whole-brain results). Full text appears complete.

The full text reports whole-brain voxelwise VBM analyses (grey matter density maps, SPM5) and regression analyses mapped to MNI space, satisfying imaging modality requirements. The sample includes a clinically diagnosed bvFTD group (n=14) and healthy controls (imaging contrasts vs. controls), meeting sample requirements (≥6 participants per group). The paper reports between-group voxelwise contrasts for bvFTD versus controls (separate from other patient groups) and whole-brain results described in the text/figures/tables. No exclusion criteria are violated (not a review; not ROI-only; empirical VBM study; no disallowed modalities). The provided full text includes introduction, methods, imaging methods, results and discussion and appears complete for screening purposes.

This study uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM) (I3) and includes a clinically diagnosed frontal-variant FTD group (FTD-fv, equivalent to bvFTD) (I4). Patient group sizes meet the minimum (25 FTD-fv patients; 22 CBS; controls n=14) (I5). The paper reports whole-brain, voxelwise between-group contrasts comparing the FTD-fv group to controls with results reported in MNI coordinates (e.g., crosshair 14,10,14) and FWE-corrected maps (I6, I7). Whole-brain results are presented in figures and described in text (I8). Full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided here, so fulltext_incomplete=false. No exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical VBM study of clinically diagnosed bvFTD with adequate sample sizes (15 patients per bvFTD stage; 45 controls), reporting whole-brain voxelwise (SPM/VBM) group contrasts with MNI coordinates and corrected statistics. Thus it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8. However, multiple participants across bvFTD groups had coexisting motor neuron disease (MND) (e.g., 5/15 in CDR 0.5, 5/15 in CDR 1, 3/15 in CDR 2–3), meaning the sample includes concurrent neurological disease. This violates exclusion criterion E7 (studies including participants with other neurological symptoms). The full text appears complete (intro, methods, results, discussion). Because any single exclusion criterion mandates exclusion, the study is excluded.

This is an empirical VBM study of bvFTD that reports whole-brain voxelwise group contrasts and correlations in standard coordinate space. The paper uses voxel‑based morphometry (VBM) as the imaging modality, includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients (N=20 total; N=17 in MRI subset) and healthy controls (N=39 total; N=28 MRI subset), and both patient and control groups exceed the 6‑participant threshold. The authors report VBM atrophy contrasts comparing bvFTD to controls and report voxelwise clusters with coordinates (MNI/Talairach) for both masked reward‑network and whole‑brain analyses. Whole‑brain voxelwise results are clearly described in the text and include coordinate data. Full text contains methods, results, and discussion. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

The study is excluded because it does not meet all required inclusion criteria I6 and I7. Met inclusion criteria: I3 (uses fMRI and voxel-based morphometry), I4 (includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients), and I5 (bvFTD group and controls meet minimum n≥6). Not met: I6 and I7 — the voxelwise structural MRI analyses combined bvFTD and PNFA into a single group for patient vs control comparisons, and no group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) contrast exclusively comparing bvFTD to controls in MNI/Talairach space is reported. The fMRI component was performed in healthy young adults only and does not provide bvFTD vs control whole-brain contrasts. No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) were triggered. Full text appears complete.

Although this study used VBM and FDG-PET and reports whole-brain voxelwise group analyses, it is excluded because it does not provide bvFTD-specific between-group contrasts. The FTLD patient sample (n=11) is a mixed group (FTD n=4, semantic dementia n=5, mixed n=2) and results are reported for the pooled FTLD group versus controls rather than for a clinically defined bvFTD (behavioral-variant FTD) subgroup. Therefore: (a) I6 is not satisfied (no between-group contrast specifically for bvFTD vs. controls in stereotactic coordinates); (b) I4 is not satisfied (bvFTD diagnosis is not clearly isolated/present as a target sample); (c) I5 is not satisfied for a bvFTD subgroup because the FTD subgroup has only 4 patients (<6). Inclusion criteria satisfied: I3 (VBM/FDG-PET used), I7 (whole-brain voxelwise results reported), I8 (results clearly described in text/figures). No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) applied. Full text appears complete.

This study meets all inclusion criteria for the review objective. It used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) as an imaging modality and explicitly reports VBM analyses (I3). The sample includes a clinically diagnosed behavioural variant FTD (bvFTD) group (n=11) (I4) and includes >=6 participants in the bvFTD group (11) and in controls (8) (I5). The paper reports between-group voxelwise contrasts in a standard stereotactic space (Talairach) comparing diagnostic groups, including bvFTD versus controls, with reported significant clusters and coordinates (I6). It provides whole-brain, group-level voxelwise VBM results clearly identified for the bvFTD group (I7), with results presented in text/tables/figures (I8). Core article content (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) is present; fulltext_incomplete=false. No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) apply. Therefore INCLUDED.

This is an original empirical neuroimaging study of clinically diagnosed probable bvFTD patients (Rascovsky criteria). It used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) on MRI and FDG-PET with voxelwise SPM5 analyses and partial-volume correction, reporting group-level whole-brain voxelwise between-group contrasts (patients vs. controls) with tables/figures in stereotactic space. Sample size is 15 bvFTD patients and 15 matched healthy controls (>=6 each). The full text contains Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. No exclusion criteria were met (not a review, not ROI-only, no comorbid psychiatric/substance cases, not non-empirical, and not only seed-based FC/DTI/cortical thickness). Therefore the paper meets all required inclusion criteria and should be INCLUDED.

This is a task-based fMRI study of clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients (n=15) versus healthy controls (n=11). It uses task fMRI (I3), includes a bvFTD sample (I4), and both patient and control groups exceed the minimum size of 6 participants (I5). The paper reports between-group contrasts in standard stereotactic space (MNI) comparing bvFTD to controls (I6) and presents at least one group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) result with FWE whole-brain correction (I7). Reporting of coordinates/figures and text descriptions satisfy acceptable reporting (I8). No exclusion criteria are met: this is empirical original research, not a review, not ROI-only, no disqualifying comorbid sample, and not limited to excluded modalities. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and should be included.

This is an empirical, longitudinal FDG-PET study of ‘frontal variant’ FTD (behavioral variant phenotype). It used whole-brain, voxelwise SPM analyses and reports between-group contrasts with Talairach coordinates comparing 22 clinically diagnosed FTD patients to 15 healthy controls. Sample sizes exceed the minimum (≥6). Whole-brain results for the target (FTD) group are clearly reported (baseline and follow-up) and coordinates/cluster maxima are provided. The full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria apply. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for the bvFTD meta-analysis.

Inclusion criteria met: I3 (uses VBM), I5 (patient group N=30 FTD and control N=14 meet sample size), I7 (reports whole-brain voxelwise SPM analyses), I8 (whole-brain results presented as statistical maps/figures). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (paper reports 'FTD' but does not specify clinically-diagnosed behavioral variant FTD or Pick's disease), I6 (no clear statement that a bvFTD-only group was compared to controls with reported coordinates in standard space). No exclusion criteria from the list (E5–E9) were violated. Therefore the study is excluded because it does not clearly include the target diagnosis (bvFTD/Pick's) required by I4 and does not definitively provide a bvFTD-specific between-group contrast as required by I6.

This study uses resting-state fMRI (meets I3), includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients within the sample (7/14; meets I4), has adequate group sizes (FTD n=14, controls n≥6; meets I5), and reports whole-brain voxelwise results with coordinates/figures in MNI space (meets I7 and I8). However, all reported between-group analyses compare the combined FTD-GRN+ group (which mixes bvFTD and avPPA cases) to controls; the paper does not present a bvFTD-only versus controls whole-brain contrast (i.e., the bvFTD group is pooled with other patients). Therefore it fails to meet I6, which requires between-group contrasts where the bvFTD group is not pooled. No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) are triggered. Full text appears complete. Exclusion is based on failure to meet I6.

This is an empirical study of clinically diagnosed behavioural variant FTD (bvFTD) that uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM) as the imaging modality and reports whole-brain, voxelwise group contrasts with MNI coordinates. Sample sizes meet thresholds (bvFTD N=26 overall; imaging subset bvFTD N=21, controls N=12; controls N=16 overall). The paper provides whole-brain VBM results (FTDp vs controls) with tables of MNI coordinates and SPM figures, and also reports ROI analyses; whole-brain results are clearly described. No exclusion criteria apply (not a review, not ROI-only, no excluded imaging modalities, and sample does not include confounding psychiatric or substance-abuse cases). Full text is complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion, tables). Therefore it meets all required inclusion criteria for the review.

This study uses VBM and includes adequate sample sizes (FTD n=37, controls present), but does not clearly meet key inclusion criteria for this bvFTD-focused review. Specifically, the FTD sample is not clearly described as clinically diagnosed behavioral-variant FTD (only 4/37 explicitly described as behavioural variant), so I4 is not satisfied. The full text does not report any between-group voxelwise contrast coordinates in a defined stereotactic space (MNI or Talairach), nor does it present clearly a group-level whole-brain voxelwise result in stereotactic coordinates; therefore I6 and I7 are not satisfied. No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) are triggered. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (VBM used) and I5 (sample sizes >=6). Inclusion criteria not met: I4, I6, I7. Consequently the study is excluded.

This empirical study used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and explicitly included a behavioral variant FTD (bvFTD) cohort (n=10) alongside healthy controls (n=10). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise contrasts between each disease group (including bvFTD) and controls, with results presented in template/MNI space (and in figures/tables). All required inclusion criteria are satisfied and no exclusion criteria apply. The provided full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so fulltext is complete.

The study is excluded because it does not report a whole-brain (voxel-wise) between-group contrast that directly compares a clinically-diagnosed bvFTD group (symptomatic carriers only) to controls. Voxel-wise analyses reported in the paper compare mutation carriers (which include both symptomatic and asymptomatic carriers) versus non-carriers rather than a bvFTD-only group. Although the paper includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients and meets several inclusion criteria (see below), the key criteria I6 and I7 are not satisfied: there is no voxel-wise, whole-brain contrast explicitly for the bvFTD (symptomatic) group vs controls—only ROI-based group comparisons among symptomatic, asymptomatic, and controls were reported. Therefore it cannot be included in the meta-analysis focused on whole-brain bvFTD vs control contrasts.

This study meets all required inclusion criteria for the bvFTD imaging meta-analysis. Imaging modality: voxel‑based morphometry (VBM) was used (I3). Sample: includes a clinically diagnosed bvFTD group (n=24) and healthy controls (n=23), meeting minimum group sizes (I4, I5). Whole‑brain, voxelwise VBM comparisons were performed between patient groups and controls (bvFTD vs controls reported) and between AD and bvFTD, with cluster-level results reported and corrected (whole‑brain evidence) (I6, I7). Results include MNI coordinates for at least some voxelwise findings and supplementary material is referenced, satisfying acceptable reporting formats (I8). No exclusion criteria are met: this is an empirical, original VBM study (not a review), it reports whole‑brain analyses (not ROI‑only), and comorbidities/alcohol abuse were exclusionary in participant selection. Full text appears complete.

This study meets all required inclusion criteria for the bvFTD imaging meta-analysis. It includes a clinically diagnosed bvFTD group (n=22) and healthy controls (n=34), both >6 participants. The paper performed voxel-based morphometry (VBM) (I3) with scans registered to MNI152 space and voxelwise whole-brain analyses (I7), reporting patient–control group comparisons (bvFTD vs. controls) that replicated the visual-rating findings; these results are referenced in the main text and in supplementary figures (I8). The VBM contrasts were conducted in standard space (MNI) and involve between-group contrasts where bvFTD is not pooled with other patient groups (I6). Sample sizes satisfy I5 and clinical diagnosis criteria satisfy I4. No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) are met. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion; supplementary figures are externally linked but acceptable, so fulltext_incomplete=false.

This is an empirical VBM study of clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients (23 patients included) with a healthy control group (20 controls). The paper reports whole-brain, voxelwise VBM group comparisons (two-sample t-test) showing atrophic clusters in bilateral anterior temporal lobes and additional regions, and voxelwise regression analyses relating behavioral measures to GM volume in the patient group. Imaging modality includes VBM (and FDG-PET performed in most patients). Sample sizes exceed the minimum (patients=23, controls=20). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise results comparing bvFTD to controls are reported. Full text contains Introduction, Methods (including VBM preprocessing and statistics), Results (behavior and imaging) and Discussion; core article content is present. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, I7 and the reporting allowance I8. No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) apply. Full text appears complete.

Full text is complete and the study is empirical, uses FDG-PET and includes clinically diagnosed frontal variant/bvFTD patients (n=13) and controls (n=21). It reports whole-brain voxelwise SPM results correlating autobiographical memory measures with resting FDG uptake in the fv-FTD group (i.e., group-level, whole-brain voxelwise results in stereotactic space). However, the paper does not present a between-group voxelwise contrast (bvFTD patients versus controls) reported in MNI/Talairach coordinates. Inclusion criterion I6 (at least one between-group contrast comparing bvFTD to controls in defined stereotactic space) is not met, so the study must be excluded. No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) apply.

Full text is complete. This fMRI resting-state study includes clinically diagnosed FTD patients (including 18 bvFTD cases) and reports whole-brain voxelwise ICA results correlating Reserve Index with functional connectivity. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (resting-state fMRI), I4 (sample includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD cases), I5 (patient subgroup size ≥6), I8 (results reported with MNI coordinates/voxelwise clusters). However, it does NOT meet I6: the paper does not report any between-group contrast comparing a bvFTD group to healthy controls (bvFTD results are not presented as a distinct between-group contrast against controls). Consequently I7 is not met for the target comparison: there are no group-level, whole-brain voxelwise results clearly identified as coming from a bvFTD vs control contrast. Because both I6 and I7 are required, the study must be excluded.

This is an empirical VBM study (voxel-based morphometry) with accompanying whole-brain voxelwise analyses comparing clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients to healthy controls. The sample includes 13 bvFTD patients and 19 controls (both >6). Methods state images were normalized to MNI space and voxelwise two-sample t-tests were performed; Results explicitly include a section “Voxel-wise comparisons between bvFTD and CN” reporting whole-brain findings. The paper therefore meets modality (VBM), target sample (bvFTD), sample size, and whole-brain between-group contrast requirements. The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion; no exclusion criteria are met (not a review; not ROI-only; no disallowed comorbid sample; not DTI-only). Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to compare clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients (n=33) with healthy controls (n=34). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise two-sample t-tests were performed in MNI space with results reported (figures and supplementary tables of coordinates) for bvFTD versus controls; cerebellar analyses used SUIT but whole-brain VBM results for the cerebral cortex are presented. The bvFTD group was not pooled with other patient groups in the reported between-group contrasts. Sample sizes exceed the minimum. Therefore all required inclusion criteria for VBM studies of bvFTD are met and no exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical study that includes clinically diagnosed bvFTD patients and uses both VBM and task-based fMRI, with patient and control group sizes >6. However, the imaging group-level voxelwise contrasts reported are comparisons between AD and bvFTD (VBM) rather than between bvFTD and healthy controls. The paper does not present a whole-brain (voxelwise) group contrast explicitly comparing bvFTD to controls in MNI/Talairach space. Therefore it fails inclusion criteria I6 (between-group contrast of bvFTD vs controls) and I7 (at least one group-level whole-brain result clearly identified as coming from the bvFTD vs control comparison). Inclusion criteria met: I3 (VBM/fMRI used), I4 (bvFTD sample), I5 (sample sizes ≥6). No exclusion criteria (E5–E9) apply. Full text appears complete. Given the missing required between-group whole-brain contrast comparing bvFTD to controls, the study must be excluded from the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical, whole-brain, voxel-wise longitudinal MRI study of frontotemporal lobar degeneration that includes a distinct bvFTD group (n=44) and controls (n=97). The methods use voxel-wise gray-matter contraction/expansion maps computed with SPM12 and DARTEL, normalized to MNI space, and report between-group t-maps and consensus voxelwise ROIs comparing bvFTD to controls. Sample sizes exceed the minimum. Whole-brain, group-level voxelwise results for bvFTD versus controls are presented (figures, maps, and effect sizes). No exclusion criteria (e.g., review-only, ROI-only, seed-based FC/DTI/cortical-thickness-only) apply. Full text (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) is provided. Therefore all required inclusion criteria (I3, I4, I5, I6, I7, I8) are met and no exclusion criteria are triggered.
